newsitem.title: USA: RTRS-October difficult for commodity funds.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-October difficult for commodity funds.

text.p: The sharp downward correction to oil prices in October, along with sharp falls in grains prices, meant it was a difficult month for funds trading physical commodity markets, analysts said.

"From the end of May through October 22, investor returns in the petroleum markets enjoyed a relatively steady upward trend, cumulating to returns of 43.9 pct, but since October 22, the recent selloff has been accompanied by losses of 9.2 pct, bringing the petroleum market investor returns to 60.1 pct year-to-date," Goldman Sachs commodity research director, Steve Strongin, said.
Last week fund performance monitor, TASS Management Inc, reported hedge and commodity funds did best in currency markets in October, rather than in physical commodity markets.
The U.S. dollar has rallied strongly in the past year, reaching a 42 month high against the yen last week, before Thursday's sharp fall.

"It's probably true that most money has been made in currencies recently, as only one commodity in CRB (Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index) has been trending well, namely oil, and that trend looks to be over for now," Merrill Lynch commodity strategist Bill O'Neill said.
"In general it's been a rough few weeks for CTAs (Commodity Trading Advisors) with lots of whipsawing markets to contend with."
The CRB fell to 12 month lows last week at 236.80, but had recovered partially to 240.48 points midmorning Monday.
The Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI), with a heavy 49 pct energy-sector weighting, saw a four week low at 201.28 points, but had recovered some ground to 207.01 points midmorning Monday.
The GSCI Total Returns Index, which reached a new record high on October 8, of 3392.59, dropped 4.6 pct in late October as grain and energy sector prices fell rapidly.

The late-October fall in oil prices was expected as the seasonal build in heating oil inventories finally began, while grain prices fell as expectations of harvest size were revised up and estimates of demand were revised down, analysts said.
"But both of these patterns now seem overdone," Strongin said.

NYMEX front month December crude oil futures were trading trading at $23.68 a barrel midmorning Monday, up from a six week low at $22.47 on November 6, after correcting sharply in late October from a December contract high of $25.80.
Nearby crude oil prices saw a six year high of $26.05 when the November contract was the front month until October 22.
However, over the past year, an investment in the front month crude oil futures, rolled over 12 times as expiration neared each month, produced a cumulative return of 100.9 pct, Strongin said.
December wheat prices were trading at 381 US cents a bushel early Monday, after seeing an 18 month low for nearby wheat at 368 cents on November 5.
Metals moved counter to trend in Octber, gaining 2.4 pct for the month, Strongin said, but gold prices have since slipped to a 19 month low at $376.80, before a partial recovery in the past few days.

But above-trend U.S. economic expansion and steady growth in European and Asian economies is likely to keep returns on commodity investments healthy, despite the sharp correction to commodity prices in October, analysts said.

"The recent selloff, much like the July sell selloff, would appear to be a good time to initiate GSCI positions or to increase the size of existing positions," Goldman Sachs commodity research director, Steve Strongin said.
"Our risk assessment suggests major surprises are likely to be positive rather than negative, especially in energy," he said.
"With a global economic growth forecast of 3.5 percent for 1997, and the bulk of that growth in non-Japan Asia and the U.S., we would expect energy demand to grow between 2.9 and 3.2 pct," he said.
